extraction.name: PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language
extraction.description: This paper introduces the task of physical commonsense reasoning and a corresponding benchmark dataset called Physical Interaction: Question Answering (PIQA). The dataset aims to evaluate natural language understanding systems on questions requiring physical commonsense, where existing large pretrained models struggle (77% accuracy) compared to humans (95% accuracy). It provides analysis about the knowledge dimensions lacking in existing models.

extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset is constructed by asking annotators to provide semantic perturbations or alternative approaches to solutions for physical goals. The goals and solutions are inspired by instructables.com, focusing on everyday situations with a preference for atypical solutions. The dataset was further cleaned of basic artifacts using the AFLite algorithm.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The dataset is inspired by instructables.com, a crowdsourced collection of instructions for doing everything from cooking to car repair. Annotators were prompted with links to instructables to inspire their annotations.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The dataset is cleaned of basic artifacts using the AFLite algorithm introduced in (Sakaguchi et al. 2020; Sap et al. 2019), which is an improvement on adversarial filtering (Zellers et al. 2018; Zellers et al. 2019b). AFLite performs a systematic data bias reduction by discarding instances whose given feature representations are collectively highly indicative of the target label. Specifically, 5,000 examples from the original dataset were used to fine-tune BERT-Large, and AFLite used an ensemble of linear classifiers on pre-computed embeddings to uncover undesirable annotation artifacts.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were prompted with links to instructables.com to inspire them. They were asked to construct two component tasks, articulate a physical goal (often centered on atypical materials), and provide a valid solution. Additionally, they were asked to provide a permutation to their own solution that makes it invalid, often subtly. Annotators were seeded with instructables from six categories (costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop) to ensure diversity. During validation, examples with low agreement were removed.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Crowdsourcing platform (likely Amazon Mechanical Turk, as indicated by 'HIT design' and 'onturkerview.com'). The interface also included a 'diff button' to highlight differences between solutions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the data. This often meant that correct examples requiring expert-level knowledge were removed. Human performance was calculated by a majority vote. Annotators were chosen to participate if they achieved >90% on a qualification HIT.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Multiple annotators for validation and human performance evaluation (majority vote).
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotator pay averaged >15$/hr according to both self-reporting onturkerview.com and timing calculations. Annotators were chosen to participate if they achieved >90% on a qualification HIT.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to enable the construction of language models useful beyond the NLP community, particularly for applications requiring physical commonsense knowledge, such as robots that interact with the world and understand natural language.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset was processed using the AFLite algorithm to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples, which are known annotation artifacts that can artificially inflate model performance. AFLite performs systematic data bias reduction by discarding instances whose feature representations are highly indicative of the target label, aiming to reduce undesirable annotation artifacts.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Manual inspection of development errors showed that some 'mistakes' were actually correct but required a web search to verify. The paper notes that automated methods trained on large web crawls may eventually surpass human performance.
